Day 44 of 100 · Linux Administration

Processes & Signals

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

Processes are running programs with identities, resources and parent-child relationships; signals are one of the operating system's ways to request or force state changes.

Architecture / mental model

parent process → child PID → scheduler/resources · signal sender → target PID → process signal handling

How it works

A process has a PID, parent, user identity, open files and runtime state. Tools such as `ps`, `pgrep`, `top` and `/proc` expose different views of that state.

Signals are not all equivalent. SIGTERM requests graceful termination and gives an application a chance to clean up; SIGKILL cannot be caught and ends the process immediately.

A service supervisor such as systemd should normally own long-running service lifecycle. Killing a child process manually can fight the supervisor, which may simply start it again.

Hands-on reference

ps -ef
pgrep -a nginx
kill -TERM PID
kill -KILL PID

Verification

Send SIGTERM to a disposable test process and observe cleanup/exit, then compare with SIGKILL only where safe. Inspect the exit status and service supervisor behavior.

Field note / gotcha

`kill` without a signal does not mean 'force kill'; it sends SIGTERM by default. The command name has encouraged generations of unnecessary SIGKILLs.

Security considerations

Process ownership controls who can signal whom. Avoid running applications as root when they only need ordinary user privileges.

What I learned

Graceful shutdown is part of reliability because abruptly stopping a process can turn an application problem into data corruption or incomplete work.
